utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This was a conference called because of what seemed to be a growing list of problems with the preparation of the case for the next stage of proceedings. The advice I've had today suggests that there has been some significant change in some matters of significance in the last 24 hours. What I might do is just call through the matters that seem to have needed attention yesterday to ensure where we're at with each of them. Firstly, there was the need to finalise the Defence witness list. As I understand it, that was done yesterday. That's the position, is it, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. We submitted our list of witnesses yesterday, witnesses that the Defence will call to testify in our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Summaries of the witnesses. I see summaries have been provided today. Are they now complete, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the summaries in relation to the first group of witnesses about to take the stand next week, hopefully, have been forwarded to the OTP. They were submitted, if I'm not mistaken, on the 22nd. And this morning we have submitted all summaries in relation to all the witnesses that the Defence would like to call during this trial. The summaries have been submitted, estimated time of testimony length, the way in which these witnesses will testify, as well as the estimate of total time that the Defence believes the examination-in-chief of these witness will take. This estimate is given at the end of our list, the list that was forwarded today, in addition to which the counts of the indictment that each of the witnesses will be testifying about have been enclosed as well as the paragraphs, the specific paragraphs of the indictment that their respective testimonies will be in relation to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Petrovic, the times estimated for each witness, do they take account of time for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The times estimated are in relation to the examination-in-chief, whereas the total number, if I'm not mistaken, it is 34 hours and 45 minutes, this does not include the time that it will take the OTP to cross-examine these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there was an outstanding expert report yesterday, but one seems to have been filed today. Is that all of your expert reports now filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, all five of them have been filed. All of them in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the exhibits, I see a list has been -- well, I'm -- we have a list filed the day before yesterday. I understand that you have provided copies of some of them to the Prosecution today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in relation to the list of exhibits that you have in front of you, copies of all documents have been filed in B/C/S. Copies of a lot of these documents have been filed in English also. According to information that I received from the interpretation and translation services unit of the Tribunal, a large amount of documents, primarily documents related to the JNA, will have been translated by Monday, and it is on Monday that the translations will be submitted to the OTP. The group of documents that you have before you, Your Honour, are documents in relation to the Croatian side. These are also being translated, and it is during the next week or the week after that these will also get translated eventually and be submitted to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask Ms. Somers. Have I correctly understood the position with respect to those issues and whether there's anything you wish to raise about them?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: First of all, good afternoon, Your Honour. The sequence of events I think is correctly represented. The dropping on the Prosecution of exhibits today, some of which will have to be used for next week, presumably, is a great problem for us. Certainly the description, I would hate to use the word "summary" as is contemplated in 65 ter (G) inasmuch as that is a reference to facts, while there are in a few or in some of these summaries which are really just a different format of the previous versions, very little fact that would assist the Prosecution in trying to cross-examine is contained. The general reference is assertion, insight, activities, but not what is contained in the assertions, what facts, what activities, et cetera, et cetera. So the vagueness puts us in a very difficult, if not impossible situation to know where things will go so we can be ready for cross. The review of the exhibits will take time to study them, to know how they apply, and beyond that, if the Chamber's question is: Does it represent the time line of events? Yes. Its impact is quite a serious concern for us. As the Chamber of course knows, generally speaking the Defence has the benefit of statements with much more information well in advance, generally. We don't have that. And in order for us effectively to conduct a cross-examination, we need to have the time frame of 65 ter give us that -- that benefit. Additionally, we had made a request I which think the Chamber is aware of. It was through correspondence, I believe, copied to the Chamber of enough identifying information. I think the J and B number may have been provided but it doesn't help us because we don't have a database that links that in. So date of birth, father's name, place of birth is at the minimum what is required to distinguish John Doe from John Doe. And it is a problem for us in that we do not have all of that information. So we are finding ourselves last minute trying to determine if perhaps information we have on a John Doe is the same John Doe. That is pretty much the state of play, and I did file in the motion to compel the relief sought. I think it's going to put us in a very difficult position to be able to move forward in the Chamber's time frame. We have tried informally as was directed to get this information without success. New that we have much of it, the ability to assimilate it adequately, to be able to put the matter to the witness while on the stand is very problematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. First of all, what I'd like to say is the following: What the Defence have filed is, in our understanding, in compliance with Rule 65 ter (G). Having read the submission by my learned friend and colleague, I didn't find it difficult to take all the documents and go through them. The OTP submission pursuant to 65 ter (G), their summaries, the summaries they provided, which are much more terse than the ones that we have actually submitted. I have them in front of me now, and there are summaries that only consist of as much as a handful of sentences, and now I have my learned friend and colleague complaining about this or that not being there. I'm not convinced that the Defence has an obligation that the OTP does not have to file our witness statements. There are no such statements. The Defence took no witness statements. It's as simple as that. There's no obligation for the Defence to take witness statements. Anyone who looks at these summaries can see for themselves. There are summaries that contain much more information than the summaries submitted by the OTP on the 12th of December last year. As for the time frame, Your Honour, we used informal channels almost two weeks ago to submit and file a list of witnesses that we believe was relevant at the time. In view of the fact that it was on the 22nd in the afternoon that we received the ruling of the Trial Chamber Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pursuant to Rule 98 bis, and it was only on the 3rd of this month in the morning that we received a complete ruling on the 98 bis, we did whatever we could to file everything that was expected of us as soon as possible. I must point out something else, too, Your Honour. All these persons who are mentioned in these documents and persons from our witness list are persons who have been referred to repeatedly in this courtroom. All these are persons that anyone who studied and examined these events is familiar with. If you look at their names, and I can elaborate on a name-to-name basis, if you'd like me to. I can tell you exactly who and when referred to these persons here during this trial, even by the OTP. These are no new names, at least in 90 per cent of the persons concerned. These are no new events or new names being referred to and brought up. These are all things that we have referred to during this trial, and their names were mentioned directly are indirectly even from the witness stand. There's nothing new there. There's no surprise being sprung on the OTP. There's no novelty involved, really. Anyone who studied this case knows who these persons are, knows who the company commanders are, and is familiar with all the names being referred to in our summaries and the remaining documents that we have filed if that's what it takes. We can go through them on a name-to-name basis and discuss. However, any claim that someone is not prepared to cross-examine someone may perhaps be an accurate claim, but what is the reason? The reason is not that the Defence team has failed to file something in a timely fashion. This claim can only be accurate if someone has failed to study the case, relying perhaps on a single witness and what this witness may or may not say once put on the stand. That is my case. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I have just a moment, please. There was no suggestion that statements from the Defence are the issue. The convenient is that the Prosecution is obligated to provide the statements and generally well in advance does so. So whatever the level of summary, the fact is the Defence has a very good idea of exactly what the witness is going to be asked about long, long in advance. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that's the nature of the burden carried by the Prosecution, I'm afraid, rather than some fault in procedures being observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Not challenged. However, in terms of equality of arms which is a concept which is well put among the Chambers, the -- the fact that what is the burden on the Defence should have at least some meaning for preparation. Whether or not a person is mentioned a hundred, one, or a thousand times during the course of the case in chief is not the issue. The question is what is it about the person that the Prosecution needs to research until the person knows -- until the Prosecution is aware that that person is in fact going to be called as a witness, the background of the individual, points for credibility are impossible to know. We are not dealing necessarily with running a search on someone who -- about whom information is readily accessible. It is a process, as the Chamber knows. We are dealing not necessarily with the facility of a domestic jurisdiction. It takes a lot to find out about witnesses. And of course on matters of credibility or credit, that is very important, so we need obviously to have the information sufficiently in advance to be able to handle that. The -- the concept of facts, I mean, yes, a name can be mentioned, but what is it? What aspect about a particular witness will be pursued by the Defence is not necessarily something that could be in the crystal ball in front of the Prosecution. And having said that, for us to be ready on Monday is just about impossible given the background to these particular points that I've raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've taken the trouble myself to look at the Prosecution's compliance with the requirement to provide summaries and compared it with what has now been provided, and I have to say that Mr. Petrovic isn't very far wide of the mark if it comes to summaries. I'm very conscious that in addition, there is a separate and distinct obligation on the Prosecution to provide the Defence with statements or proofs, but if one is comparing summary to summary, I think you will well understand that there's force in what has been put by Mr. Petrovic. I might say that if one approached the question of what is a summary of evidence afresh, without the experience of what has happened in this and many other trials, one might expect something more than is to be found in what the Defence has provided, and a very great deal more in what was to be found in what the Prosecution provided. But if one has regard to what seems to be the general practice in the Tribunal, it's difficult to say that the summaries now provided are a failure to comply with the Rule. I well know how important it would be for the Defence to be in a better position to cross-examine -- I should say for the Prosecution to be in a better position to know how to approach its cross-examination if it had at least an outline of the main points to be made by a witness, but that is not, I think, the function and requirement of the Rules. The Prosecution has to accept that when it comes to cross-examine a witness, the witness may be introducing evidence of which the Prosecution has no knowledge and has had no notice. So the burden is a heavier one than lies on the Defence in this respect, because if the Defence is taken by surprise by some material aspect of the Prosecution evidence, there has been a non-compliance with the Rules by the Prosecution which provides a more sure foundation for some remedial action by the Trial Chamber. The identification of witnesses, I see, can be a problem, but from what I saw of the witness list, many of these are former military people who held some rank of significance in the armed forces, so that it's not as though you're going to be confronted, for the most part, by people who simply come out of nowhere. These are people who were on stage, as it were, although they may not have been the centre of your particular attention in preparation. It's fair to say, though, that what has been done, Mr. Petrovic, falls in time, in particular, significantly short of what might normally be expected, and it has undoubtedly presented problems for the Prosecution greater than ought to have been. This was anticipated when we adjourned some weeks ago, and the Chamber urged the parties and received from each of them an assurance that there would be informal cooperation to avoid the sort of situation that has occurred. It's a particular disappoint to me that very little has happened until the last few days. I know that you say, "Well, we didn't have the 98 bis decision," but the preparation of the Defence case didn't need to stand still until the 98 bis decision was delivered, which appears to have been the course that has been followed. My assessment on balance is that the case should proceed next week as planned. I do recognise that there could well be, with a particular witness or over a particular issue, a real problem caused by the short notice, a problem greater than the Prosecution should be asked to carry. Should that occur in respect of any particular witness and if the Chamber is satisfied of that at the time, then there will, could I say, be a clear basis upon which the Prosecution could seek to have the whole or part of its cross-examination deferred at least until the end of the witness that follows to give more time. Now, do not take from that that it can be expected that there will be a deferment of all cross-examinations virtually as a course. It will be a matter of assessing the circumstances and seeing whether that course becomes necessary in the view of the Chamber, so that you may find it difficult to persuade the Chamber in a particular case that there is really justification for the adjournment. But if the Chamber is satisfied, that, in my present assessment of the matter, ought to provide a means of allowing the Prosecution reasonable opportunity to overcome the sort of problem that could well loom as we go through the evidence. A consequence of that, Mr. Petrovic, or two consequences of that occur to me immediately. There may be more. The first is that some Defence witnesses may well need to wait in The Hague longer than might otherwise have been expected. The second is that you may need to have the next witness ready earlier than you expected if there is a matter which justifies deferral in part or whole of the cross-examination of a particular witness. So that will have to be borne in mind as you proceed. Now, clearly the occasion for this will diminish as the case proceeds, because time will have run by then, although that naturally will mean that the resources of the Prosecution will be under pressure. I think that's all I can say about those matters at the moment, Ms. Somers, unless there's something more that you seek to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wanted to ask Your Honour. You raised a point about possibly some -- I think you raised a point, at least I inferred it, that perhaps some form of point summary might be of assistance. In other words, if some Chambers do, we did not always --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was merely reflecting back on what I would have loved at times that I have prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I would loved to have had my hand before I had to cross-examine. You will pardon a Judge for reflecting back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No. I reflect back to other days as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There were times I had been defendant and felt I hadn't been given a proper deal either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We all share that experience, but I would say under the circumstances perhaps if the Chamber is minded it might be helpful to have at least a point summary of the areas of inquiry which I don't think is terribly burdensome inasmuch as in different Chambers we've had to do it as well. And a day -- at least a day in advance of it would be helpful. Again it varies from Chamber to Chamber but perhaps it might alleviate the circumstances and avoid unnecessary delays. It would direct us perhaps a bit better, and for all parties it might be a better -- or a helpful solution, and we would be very grateful for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, a suggestion has been put forward which may help minimise any possible need for delay in the dealing with the witness and therefore ease some of the consequential problems that could arise for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately I find that what my learned friend and colleague has put forward would amount to no more than they already have in these summaries. What my learned friend and colleague refers to has been done on their part, as we can remember, and it's important to note when that document was delivered. It was on the 16th of January this year, which is a full month after the beginning of the trial. So I must say again the document I'm referring to is the OTP indictment proofing chart, which is really what my learned colleague is expecting to have. It was forwarded on the 16th of January. And we had begun on the 15th of December. Therefore, Your Honour, we shall do our best could comply with whatever rulings you may make, but we can't be sure that this will necessarily be useful to the other side since the subjects we are about to tackle are very narrow and restricted. Our view of our defence case is to focus as narrowly as we can on a specific development, and there is only one true development, and all these witnesses will be speaking about will for the most cases be focused on that one development. Therefore, anything beyond that would be inopportune in our view. However, Your Honour, we are in our hands and we shall comply with whatever you decide with a view to expedite these proceedings and bring them to a speedy end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I put this to you Mr. Petrovic: My viewing of what has been provided by the Defence by way of summary leaves me with very little understanding of what a witness is going to speak about. There is an indication that the witness may give an account of his role on the 6th of December, or words to that effect, but no indication of what the witness was doing on the 6th, how his evidence will be material to the events, at what points his witness -- his evidence will differ from other evidence in the case. They are the matters, as you will well understand, upon which the Prosecution would prefer to concentrate and leave all others aside. That will save time for everybody. That's just the material matters. Now, your summary doesn't summarise that evidence at all. It merely, as it were, gives a heading of what the witness might be talking about but doesn't summarise at all what it is the witness is going to say in the evidence. Now, I've heard you say that you have no witness statements from any witness. I will make no observation about that at this point, but you certainly must have an idea what it is the witness is going to speak about, and it certainly must be within your capacity, I would think within a few minutes dealing with each of the witnesses, for example, you expect to call in the coming week to give some indication of the nature of the evidence that witness is going to give which you see to be material to the case. Now, I think that would go quite a long way to helping the Prosecution cope with the problem that has now been set for them by the shortness of notice and the nature of the summaries that you have provided. Could I ask you to attempt to deal with that matter forthwith?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if that is your request, we shall try to comply with that request to the best of our ability. This is all I can say. Furthermore, I assume that this is only in relation to the first couple of witnesses. As for the remaining witnesses, I believe the OTP has ample time to obtain whatever information they deem necessary. This proposal of yours, Your Honour, with all due respect, I think means more than our obligation under Rule 65 ter in relation to summaries. The practice that I am familiar with, I may be mistaken, but the practice that I am familiar with does not make any such requirements. However, if that is your decision, if that is your request, we are prepared to compile some -- something like that in relation to our first witnesses. However, facing the workload that we are and that we are likely to be facing over the following weeks, this is an extra burden being placed on our shoulders. We have a three-men Defence team dealing with all the problems, the passports, looking at the citizenships of our prospective witnesses, taking care of all the procedures, getting witnesses photographed for their passports, compiling all these documents, all this paperwork. All this red tape is something that we have to deal with, and we are a team of three men. We are not complaining about this. That is not our intention by any means, but we would not like any burden being placed on us that is not strictly within the rules. However, if that is what you require, Your Honour, we shall do our best to comply with this request. Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I indicate to you, Mr. Petrovic, that my understanding of what I'm requiring is to urge you to make a part compliance with the requirement to provide a summary. I have accepted and you've heard what I've said about the nature of the summaries provided to you. It must be observed, however, that not only did you have a summary and not only did the Chamber have a summary but that there was provided in addition effectively a full statement or proof. A summary was merely something to be read in conjunction with the full statement so that you had no doubt, having read that evidence, what it was that you were going to have to deal with. Now, the Prosecution has no right to be in that same position, but that then places greater need for a reasonable compliance with the obligation to provide what is truly a summary rather than simply, as it were, a head-note of what the evidence might be. Now, we could debate all day every day exactly what might be compliance with an obligation to provide a summary. Views as to that would differ from case to case, from witness to witness, and could well differ from Trial Chamber to Trial Chamber. I don't see that what I'm putting to you is in any way requiring you to go beyond the requirement of the Rule, and in fact, as I've indicated, I think I may be allowing you to get away with something that falls short, although by no means as far short of compliance with the Rule as that which is presently being done. I'm doing that in the hope that it will enable the Prosecution to prepare adequately for its task in addition to the preparation that their whole familiarity with the case must have ensured. So that's the obligation that I'm asking, that you measure up to in a better way than at the moment. It will be essential that something be provided even today in respect of the first witness and that as soon as possible you deal with the following witnesses. The obligation is not going to stop after just one week's witnesses because of the nature of what you have presently provided as summaries. Now, I'm not suggesting you provide an exhaustive outline of what each witness is going to give, but I think you can readily appreciate that if you were being truly offered a summary of a witness's evidence, you would expect at the end of reading it to have some idea of the main points which that witness is going to speak about and the nature of where that evidence may be significantly different from anything else that is known or entirely new to the case. And that's the sort of thing that's quite missing at the moment and leaves the Prosecution simply without any idea of what it is that must be faced. So have I made my expectation clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I add that I don't think it will take a great deal of time if you do know what it is you're calling the witness for. You will be able to give a very brief indication of that in short time on your part so as not to impede heavily into the many other obligations that I well appreciate you have. Now, there are a couple of other matters, I think. You sought ex parte the issue of a witness subpoena, Mr. Petrovic. It may be done ex parte. Can I indicate that a witness subpoena will issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want to call one witness by videolink. Until we see who it is and why, I can't really presume to deal with that at the moment, so that we'll have to wait until you've made a -- at least a brief formal application.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have already announced my intention to do so to your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, is there some matter that is outstanding from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is on the -- Your Honour, it is on the issue of exhibits, and we have -- we've been served with copies of them. Now, the Rule doesn't necessarily indicate the linkage of particular exhibits to particular counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If -- and -- you know, I wish we could extract it a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I can be two paces ahead of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I understand. The point many I'm raising is because of the timing of them I've got 85 exhibits I've got to wade through. And some may be self-evident; some may not. Because some, they will be cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Most of them tended to shout.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Some I haven't seen; I just got them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm a day ahead of you. I'm sure I'll not find it hard to see what each one is dealing with and see how they fit into the picture. Some I wouldn't pretend to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If there is such a question, if we can indulge, then perhaps if in a summary it might be indicated that a particular exhibit in the point summary that may be provided of a particular -- it may be relied upon that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The description of each intended exhibit is generally quite fulsome. In that area, I don't think there's much room for complaint. It's quite obvious from the number of witnesses and the time needed for their examination-in-chief that we will be needing to be very conscious of time as the case progresses, and I would ask counsel to keep that in mind. The 98 bis decision may have had the advantage of helping to focus attention on what seems to be some of the more material issues, and that may help both counsel teams to be more directed and relevant in the areas that are explored both in the evidence in chief and cross-examination. If there's no other matter -- there is. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the nature of that issue, can we please go into closed session for a moment, please. Rather, private session. This is one of the witnesses from our list who has a peculiar problem, and this is something I would like to bring up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.08 p.m.
